Daniel is gesturing at a real and fertile idea—fixed-point theorems applied to learned representations—but the claim, as stated, rests on several hidden assumptions that are doing nearly all the work. First, the relevant theorem is almost certainly [Brouwer’s fixed-point theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brouwer_fixed-point_theorem), not “Brownian”: it guarantees a fixed point for a *continuous* function from a *compact convex* set to itself. That “to itself” condition is the biggest blind spot here. “Take an image, encode it, decode it, and compare to the top-left corner” is not (yet) a self-map on a single space unless Daniel precisely defines a state space whose elements contain both (i) a full image and (ii) a corresponding top-left patch (or some standardized embedding of patches) and then defines a continuous update rule on that joint space. Otherwise, it’s a relation across different-dimensional objects (full images vs. corners), and fixed-point machinery simply doesn’t attach.

Second, even granting a well-defined self-map, the compactness/convexity requirements are not innocent in ML settings. Typical latent spaces are \(\mathbb{R}^d\) (non-compact), typical image spaces are effectively discrete (pixels), and “encoder/decoder” pipelines include non-continuities in practice (quantization, clipping, argmax sampling). You can sometimes rescue Brouwer by restricting attention to a bounded latent ball and assuming the model maps it into itself, but that restriction is a substantive modeling claim—not something “(assume continuous space)” automatically buys. This is exactly why applied fixed-point arguments in ML often end up either (a) proving existence only for idealized, bounded, continuous surrogates, or (b) shifting to approximate fixed points (which can be meaningful empirically, but are a different claim).

A more interesting reframing Daniel’s post invites is: what does a “corner-matching fixed point” *mean* as a property of a representation? If you formalize a self-map (say, a map that replaces the whole image with a decoded version of the encoded corner, or a map on latent codes induced by a corner-extractor), you’re really studying *self-consistency constraints* between local patches and global reconstructions—closer in spirit to equilibrium models and implicit layers than to a one-off existence result. That line of thought could connect to the broader fixed-point view of deep networks (and when it fails) without overclaiming a theorem where the prerequisites are not yet pinned down.
